title: Resources and Wealth
objective: After this level you can explain how resources like oil, metals and water shape where wealth is found.
summary: Venezuela has the most proven oil; Congo mines most cobalt. Yet resource wealth often means slower growth, unless reinvested, as in Botswana. Fresh water is scarce everywhere.

cards.headline: The country with the most proven oil in the ground is not Saudi Arabia.
cards.body: It's Venezuela. And owning buried treasure, it turns out, is a very different thing from getting rich off it.

cards.headline: Treasure is unevenly spread
cards.body: Nature did not share out its resources fairly. Venezuela holds the world's largest proven crude oil reserves, ahead of Saudi Arabia. The Democratic Republic of the Congo mines about three-quarters of the world's cobalt. Rocks formed where they formed, long before anyone drew the borders of Level 93 around them.

cards.headline: The resource curse
cards.body: You'd expect a country sitting on oil or minerals to be rich. Often it isn't. Economists call this the resource curse: countries with abundant natural resources often grow more slowly than countries with fewer. One reason is conflict: when a treasure is worth fighting over, people fight over it.

cards.headline: Botswana's way out
cards.body: The curse is a pattern, not a law. Botswana relies heavily on diamond exports, yet it's widely seen as having dodged it. The trick: money from minerals is reinvested, in infrastructure, health and education. A mine empties eventually. A well-built road and an educated workforce keep paying out.

mascot.line: Keep this: the resource curse is a pattern, not a law. Reinvesting is Botswana's way out.

cards.fact: Earth is covered in water, but very little of it is drinkable.
cards.context: Remember Level 1: about 71% of Earth's surface is water. Yet the oceans hold about 96.5% of all Earth's water, and it's salty. Of the fresh water, over 68% is locked in ice and glaciers. The one resource every person needs is the one the planet keeps mostly salted or frozen.

questions.prompt: Why is Botswana often called an exception to the resource curse?
